opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it started with a fascination with how complex biological systems are. When I was a graduate student, I was trained in machine learning, and I kept running into these beautiful methods that were being applied to fairly clean, well-defined problems. Then I started looking at biological data, things like gene expression measurements across thousands of genes in many patients, and I realized that this was a setting where the problems were genuinely hard and genuinely important. You have very high-dimensional data, relatively few samples, a lot of noise, and underneath it all there's this intricate regulatory machinery that we don't fully understand.

What really drew me in was the sense that machine learning could do more than just make predictions there. In biology and medicine, a prediction by itself often isn't enough. If a model tells you a patient is likely to respond to a certain drug, a clinician or a biologist immediately wants to know why. Which genes, which pathways, which molecular features are driving that? So for me the appeal was the combination: using machine learning to uncover the underlying mechanisms of disease, and making the models interpretable enough that they actually produce biological insight people can act on.

Over time that grew into a broader interest in explainable AI, because I saw that the same need for understanding "why" applies across healthcare, whether you're looking at cancer genomics, Alzheimer's disease, or clinical data in the operating room. Computational biology was really the place where I first felt how much that mattered.

r001.rationale: The response describes applying machine learning to gene-expression data and says the appeal was using it to uncover underlying mechanisms of disease.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you so much for having me. So, I actually came to this from the machine learning side first. My PhD was in computer science, and I was working on things like structured learning and sparse models, and at some point I realized that biology was this incredible source of problems where the data was exploding but the tools to make sense of it really weren't there yet.

What really drew me in was the scale and the messiness of it. If you think about gene expression data, or now single-cell data, you have tens of thousands of genes measured across many samples, and the number of samples is almost always much smaller than the number of features. That's exactly the regime where naive machine learning fails, and where you need to think carefully about priors, about structure, about what biological knowledge you can bring in. For someone who loves methods, that's a really exciting place to be, because the biology forces you to invent new things rather than just apply what's off the shelf.

But the other piece, and this became more and more important to me over time, is that in biology and medicine, prediction alone is not the goal. A model that predicts which patients will respond to a drug is useful, but a clinician or a biologist wants to know why. Which genes, which pathways, which features are actually driving that prediction? So very early on I became interested in interpretability, in explainable AI, because in this domain the explanation is often the scientific discovery. The model is a means to generate hypotheses that you can go back and test in the lab or in the clinic.

And I think that's what has kept me here. There's this feedback loop where the biology motivates new machine learning, and the machine learning actually changes what questions biologists can ask. When those two sides are talking to each other, it's really hard to imagine working on anything else.

r001.rationale: The response says gene-expression data drew her to machine learning and emphasizes finding genes or pathways that explain predictions, but it does not say she was drawn to using it to identify causes of diseases.

astra-6.text:
What drew me in was the possibility of finding meaningful patterns in biological data that would be very difficult to see otherwise. Biology presents these incredibly complex questions, and machine learning gives us a way to approach that complexity systematically.

But the exciting part for me isn’t just making an accurate prediction. It’s understanding what the model has learned. If a model can predict something about a disease, can we use it to uncover which biological factors matter and generate hypotheses that we can test? That connection between computation and biological understanding is what really interests me.

r001.rationale: The response says machine learning can find patterns in biological data and identify biological factors related to disease, but it does not specify gene-expression data or clearly state that the goal is to identify causes of diseases.

sol-6.1.text:
What drew me in was the possibility of finding patterns in biological data that could help us understand human health. Biology is incredibly complex, and machine learning offers a way to study how many factors interact, rather than looking at one factor at a time.

But for me, making an accurate prediction is only part of the goal. We also want to understand why a model makes that prediction. If it predicts a disease, what biological signals is it using? Can those signals help us develop a new hypothesis? That connection between computation and biological discovery is what makes this area so exciting to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes using machine learning to find patterns in biological data and explore disease predictions, but it does not specify gene-expression data or identifying disease causes.
